title: Speculate While You Reason: Teaching Agents to Predict Their Next Tool Call via Joint Agent-Speculator RL
event_hint: Self-speculating agent: single-model tool-call speculation via joint agent-speculator RL
problem: LLM agents spend substantial wall-clock time waiting for tool call results (remote services, network I/O, sub-agent invocations). Prior tool-call speculation approaches use external draft models or cached traces that suffer from the 'speculator-agent gap': conditioned on the same trajectory, the speculator and the deployed agent choose different next tool calls. External speculators also add serving overhead (extra model weights, separate KV cache).
mechanism: A single LLM operates in two modes sharing the same parameters and prefix KV cache. In agent mode it follows the standard agentic trajectory (reasoning, tool calls, observations, answers). In speculator mode, the same model receives the intermediate trajectory prefix plus a fixed speculation suffix and directly predicts the next structured tool call (tool name + argument dictionary). Joint agent-speculator RL trains both modes: at each iteration, agent rollouts are sampled, speculation pairs are constructed from realized tool-call turns, and a fixed schedule alternates agent and speculator DAPO updates. Key stabilization: (1) SFT warmup on successful trajectories + speculation examples, (2) optimizer state reset at mode switches, (3) 4:8 agent:speculator update schedule, (4) penalty for repeated meaningless tool calls. The speculation reward is name-conditioned: tool-name must match, then macro token-F1 over argument keys.

evidence.claim: Joint agent-speculator RL improves average next tool-call Hit@1 from 44.1 to 61.2 for Qwen3-4B and from 48.9 to 66.3 for Qwen3.5-4B
evidence.condition: Averaged over HotpotQA, MuSiQue, BCP, tau-bench Airline/Retail; Hit@1 requires exact tool-name + full argument-dictionary match

evidence.claim: Self-speculation outperforms external draft models: the target 4B agent prompted to predict its own next call already beats smaller same-family draft models
evidence.source_locator: Table 1: Qwen3-4B self reaches 25.3/37.2 Hit@1 on MuSiQue/tau-bench vs 14.7/25.4 for Qwen3-1.7B
evidence.condition: 50 evaluation queries, online speculation during agent rollout, single H100 GPU

evidence.claim: Task success is preserved after RL: average success changes from 26.6 to 27.7 for Qwen3-4B and from 49.2 to 50.6 for Qwen3.5-4B
evidence.condition: No systematic degradation across search QA or conversational tool-use benchmarks

evidence.claim: External speculators add memory and latency overhead: Qwen3-4B on MuSiQue increases from 8.70GB/8.3s (self) to 10.71GB/27.4s (Qwen3-0.6B)
evidence.source_locator: Table 1 and Section 2.2 'External speculators add serving overhead'
evidence.condition: GPU memory includes model weights and peak KV-cache; single H100 GPU, SGLang inference

evidence.claim: The 4:8 agent:speculator update schedule achieves the best results vs 1:1: 55.2 avg Hit@1 and 26.1 avg success vs 31.8/10.3 for 1:1
evidence.source_locator: Table 4: Ablation over agent:speculator update schedules on SearchQA
evidence.condition: Same iteration budget; SearchQA with Qwen3-4B; speculator needs enough consecutive signal to track agent's call distribution

evaluation_context: Two task families: Agentic SearchQA (HotpotQA, MuSiQue, BrowseComp-Plus) requiring multi-hop search + reasoning, and tau-bench (Airline, Retail) requiring conversational tool-use with schema-constrained APIs. Backbones: Qwen3-4B and Qwen3.5-4B. RL: DAPO-style grouped policy optimization, G_ag=8, G_sp=8, lr 3e-6, 200-step budget. Hardware: 8 H100 GPUs (SearchQA), 8 H200 GPUs (ToolScale). Inference: SGLang engine. Training data: FlashQA (283,338 train), ToolScale (4,063 train). Metric: Hit@1 exact match (tool name + complete argument dictionary).
limitations: Assumes speculative tool calls can be issued without changing the external environment — suitable only for read-only tools (search, retrieval, lookup); NOT suitable for mutating/irreversible operations (placing orders, DB updates, sending messages) without additional safeguards. Evaluated only on 4B-scale models; larger models may exhibit different optimization dynamics. Only two task families tested — code execution, web navigation, long-running workflows, and multi-agent tool use are not covered. Cross-domain generalization (Table 3) shows task success drops when trained on one domain and tested on another (e.g., SearchQA-trained model on tau-bench: success 21.6/36.4 to 17.6/29.8). No end-to-end wall-clock latency reduction measured — Hit@1 is a proxy for potential latency hiding.
project_relevance: Directly addresses 'parallel-speculative tool calls' for agent acceleration. The self-speculation design that fully reuses prefix KV cache connects to KVCache transfer/reuse research — the speculation branch adds only a small suffix, avoiding a second model or separate cache. The joint RL methodology (alternating agent/speculator updates with optimizer resets) could inform training models for speculative execution in broader inference-network contexts. The speculator-agent gap finding (the agent is its own best speculator) challenges the external-draft-model paradigm. For coding agents specifically, the read-only restriction is significant — file reads and searches are safe to speculate, but edits and test runs are not, which limits applicability to the planning/exploration phase of coding tasks. Inference: if Hit@1 reaches ~60-66%, roughly two-thirds of read-only tool latencies could be hidden, but the exact-match requirement means argument-level accuracy is the binding constraint.
